summary: This short document updates RFC 7854, the BGP Monitoring Protocol, by changing registration procedures for several registries. Any BMP registry with a range of 32768-65530 marked Specification Required now has that range set to First Come First Served.

plainLanguage.summary: A club's sign-up sheet had strict rules for part of the list. This part is now open, first come, first served.

questions: bmp registry first come first served
subtitle: Simplifies registration procedures for BGP Monitoring Protocol IANA registries.

tldr.problem: BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) registries had strict registration rules (Specification Required) for code points 32768-65530, which delayed allocation and increased the risk of unregistered code points being used informally.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9515 changes six BMP registries so that the 32768-65530 range uses First Come First Served instead of Specification Required, allowing faster allocation with minimal review.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now quickly register new monitoring extensions without waiting for RFC approval, reducing pressure to use unregistered code points.

today: RFC 9515 is the current standard. All BMP implementations should follow its registration procedures when allocating new monitoring code points.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
RFC 7854 created the BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) and defined several IANA registries for code points. These registries included two ranges: one requiring Specification Required (strict approval) and another requiring Standards Action (full RFC process). In practice, the high-value range 32768-65530 with Specification Required was almost never used because the burden of getting a specification published was too high.

This created pressure for operators to use unregistered code points unofficially, risking collisions when multiple vendors independently chose the same values.
sections.plainLanguage: There was a waiting list to add new things, and the waiting process was so strict that nobody used it officially. People started using secret code points instead.

sections.title: First Come First Served Registration
sections.content:
RFC 9515 changes six registries: BMP Statistics Types, Initiation and Peer Up TLVs, Termination Message TLVs, Termination Message Reason Codes, Route Mirroring TLVs, and Route Mirroring Information Codes. For each registry, the 32768-65530 range now uses First Come First Served instead of Specification Required.

First Come First Served is a registration policy defined in RFC 8126 that requires only basic checks (is the code point available? does the request make sense?) and does not require publication of an RFC or specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of saying yes or no to formal applications, the registrar now just checks if the number is free and approves it. It takes minutes instead of months.

sections.title: Impact on Network Monitoring
sections.content: This change makes BMP more useful for proprietary and experimental extensions. Organizations can now quickly reserve code points for their own monitoring probes or for features still in development. The lower bar for registration is balanced by keeping the highest ranges (Standards Action) for features that must be widely interoperable.
sections.plainLanguage: Network teams can now try new monitoring ideas without waiting for approval committees. When an idea proves useful, it can still be formalized later.
